name: Additive (Bahdanau) attention
title_check: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
plain: Before this, a translator had to cram a whole sentence into one small summary before writing anything, and long sentences fell apart. This let it look back at every word of the original as it wrote, at the cost of running a little scoring network on every pair of words.
problem: An encoder-decoder RNN squeezed the entire source sentence into one fixed-size vector, so translation quality collapsed as sentences got longer.
mechanism: Instead of one final hidden state, keep every encoder state. At each decoding step, score each of them with a small feed-forward network, softmax the scores into weights, and read out a weighted sum.
buys: Removes the fixed-size bottleneck; long sentences stop degrading
Produces an interpretable soft alignment between source and target words
Works with any encoder length without architectural change
costs: The scoring MLP is a learned module evaluated for every (query, key) pair — more expensive per pair than a dot product
Still bolted onto an RNN, so the sequential bottleneck remains
Cost is already quadratic in the pairs considered, it just was not the binding constraint yet
pick_when: Historical interest only. Its idea survives everywhere; its implementation survives nowhere.

name: Multiplicative (Luong) attention
title_check: Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
plain: The same idea, but the scoring is a plain multiplication instead of a small neural network. Much faster on a graphics card and slightly weaker when the vectors are small, and this is the version that survived.
problem: Bahdanau's additive scorer was a whole neural network run per pair, which is slow and hard to batch.
mechanism: Replace the scoring MLP with a plain dot product (optionally with a learned matrix in the middle). Scoring becomes a single matrix multiply.
buys: Scoring collapses to one GEMM, which GPUs are extremely good at
Fewer parameters than the additive scorer
This is the direct ancestor of the dot-product attention used today
costs: Dot products grow with vector dimension, so scores can get large and saturate the softmax — the exact problem the 1/√d scaling later fixes
Slightly worse than additive attention at small dimensions
Still attached to an RNN
pick_when: Historical interest, but this is the moment attention became a matrix multiply, which is why it won.

name: Learned absolute position embeddings
title_check: Convolutional Sequence to Sequence Learning
authors: Gehring, Auli, Grangier, Yarats, Dauphin (Facebook AI Research)
plain: Keep a lookup table with one vector per slot number and add it to each word, so the model knows the order. Simple, but the table runs out: train on 1024 slots and slot 1025 has no entry at all.
problem: Once you drop recurrence, the model has no idea what order the tokens are in — attention is permutation-invariant. Something must tell it.
mechanism: Keep a lookup table with one learned vector per position, and add it to the token embedding at the input. Position 5 always gets the same vector.
buys: Trivially simple: one embedding table, added once at the input
The model can learn whatever positional structure the data actually contains, rather than a shape chosen by a human
Zero cost inside the attention loop
costs: Hard-capped at the trained length. Position 4097 in a 4096-trained model has no vector at all — it cannot extrapolate, it simply has no entry
Encodes absolute position, not relative distance, so the model must learn 'these are 3 apart' separately for every pair of absolute positions
Costs parameters proportional to max sequence length
The signal is added at the input and must survive every layer without being overwritten
pick_when: Short, fixed-length inputs where you will never exceed the training length — classification heads, encoders over capped-length text. Never for a model you intend to extend.
confused_with: Often attributed to BERT or to the Transformer paper. Both used it, but it appears earlier, in ConvS2S.

name: Scaled dot-product attention (softmax attention)
title_check: Attention Is All You Need
authors: Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin (Google)
plain: Every word asks a question, every word wears a label, and how well a question matches a label decides how much of that word gets read. It is exact and it looks everywhere, which is precisely why it costs so much.
problem: Recurrence forces computation to happen one step at a time, which wastes a GPU. Could attention alone carry the whole model?
mechanism: Every token is projected three ways: a query (what am I looking for), a key (what do I offer), a value (what I actually pass on). Score every query against every key with a dot product, divide by √d, softmax into weights that sum to one, and read out a weighted sum of values. This is the baseline everything else is measured against.
math: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q Kᵀ / √d_k ) V
math_note: As published. The √d_k is not cosmetic: without it, dot products in high dimensions grow large, the softmax saturates towards one-hot, and gradients through it vanish.
buys: Fully parallel across the sequence — the entire attention matrix is computed in one matmul
Constant path length between any two tokens: position 1 and position 100000 are one hop apart
Exact. No approximation, no forgetting, no eviction — every token can see every previous token at full fidelity
The softmax creates genuine competition between tokens, and each query gets a fresh distribution over all keys
costs: Time and memory are O(n²) in sequence length. Doubling context quadruples the attention cost
At inference every past key and value must be cached, and that cache grows linearly with tokens and with concurrent users — this is the bill that drives most of the timeline below
Permutation-invariant on its own, so it needs a separate positional scheme bolted on
The 1/√d scaling is load-bearing: without it, dot products in high dimensions grow large, the softmax saturates, and gradients vanish
pick_when: The default, and still correct for anything up to a few thousand tokens where exactness matters more than throughput. Every mechanism below is a way of paying less than this — and each one gives something up to do it.
confused_with: Commonly dated to 2018. The arXiv v1 is 12 June 2017; NeurIPS publication is December 2017. There is no 2018 version.

name: Multi-head attention (MHA)
title_check: Attention Is All You Need
plain: Run several attentions side by side on different slices of each word, so one can follow grammar while another follows the topic. Splitting itself is free in both arithmetic and memory; the expense is that nothing is shared between the slices, which leaves a great deal to claw back later.
problem: A single softmax attention distribution has to average everything it wants to attend to. One head cannot simultaneously track syntax and long-range topic.
mechanism: Split the embedding into h slices, run independent attention on each with its own Q/K/V projections, concatenate the results and project back. Each head can specialise in a different relation.
math:
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head₁, …, head_h) Wᴼ
        head_i     = Attention(Q W_iQ, K W_iK, V W_iV)
math_note: As published. Note that h · d_head = d_model, so the heads partition the embedding rather than duplicating it.
buys: Multiple attention patterns at once, instead of one averaged compromise
Costs no extra FLOPs versus one full-width head, since the dimension is split rather than duplicated
Heads demonstrably specialise, which makes some behaviour interpretable
costs: Stores keys and values at the full model width, for every layer and every token, because nothing is shared between heads. Worth stating precisely: the heads divide the embedding rather than duplicating it, so head count does not multiply the cache - it is the absence of sharing that costs, and that is exactly what MQA, GQA and MLA reclaim.
Heads are provably redundant; many can be pruned after training with little loss, meaning you paid to train capacity you did not need
Splitting the embedding means each head works in a lower-dimensional space
pick_when: Still the quality ceiling, and correct when memory is not your constraint — training, or short-context inference. For serving, its KV cost is why GQA exists.

name: Sinusoidal position encoding
title_check: Attention Is All You Need
plain: Rather than memorising a vector for each position, compute one from sine waves, so even slot 50,000 has an answer. Having an answer is not the same as it being useful, and quality still falls away past the length it was trained on.
problem: A learned position table cannot represent a position it never saw in training. Could position be computed instead of learned?
mechanism: Build the position vector from sine and cosine waves at geometrically spaced frequencies. Position 5000 has a well-defined encoding whether or not you trained on it, and offsets correspond to a fixed linear transform.
math:
PE(pos, 2i)   = sin( pos / 10000^(2i/d_model) )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i/d_model) )
math_note: As published. Geometrically spaced frequencies, so low dimensions turn quickly and high dimensions turn slowly.
buys: Defined at every position, including ones never trained on — no lookup table to run off the end of
Zero parameters
Relative offsets are expressible as a linear function of the encoding, which in principle lets the model learn distance
costs: Being *defined* past the training length is not the same as *working* past it — extrapolation quality degrades badly in practice, which is the whole reason ALiBi and RoPE exist
Still added at the input, so the positional signal has to survive every layer
Empirically roughly on par with learned embeddings, so it bought portability rather than accuracy
pick_when: Largely superseded by RoPE. Worth understanding because it is the first attempt at a positional scheme that is computed rather than memorised, which is the idea RoPE gets right.

name: Relative position representations
title_check: Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations
plain: Stop telling the model “you are at position 812” and start telling it “you are three words apart”, since distance is what language actually cares about. The cost is storing a value for every pair of positions.
problem: Language mostly cares that two words are three apart, not that they sit at absolute positions 812 and 815. Absolute schemes make the model learn that fact separately at every offset.
mechanism: Drop the input-level position vector. Instead, add a learned embedding indexed by the *distance* between query and key directly into the attention computation, with distances clipped beyond some window.
buys: Encodes exactly the quantity that matters — relative distance
Generalises across absolute positions: 'three apart' is one thing to learn, not one per location
Injected inside attention, so the signal cannot be washed out by intermediate layers
costs: Materialises an extra tensor over position pairs, adding real memory and time to every attention layer
Distances are clipped, so beyond the clip everything looks equally far away
Slower than absolute schemes, which delayed its adoption
pick_when: Superseded by RoPE and ALiBi, which get relative position without the per-pair tensor. Important as the conceptual bridge: this is where the field decided relative beats absolute.

name: Transformer-XL recurrence + relative encoding
title_check: Transformer-XL: Attentive Language Models Beyond a Fixed-Length Context
authors: Dai, Yang, Yang, Carbonell, Le, Salakhutdinov
plain: Keep the previous chunk's work around so context is not thrown away at the boundary and the model does not restart cold. What it keeps is slightly out of date, and it grows.
problem: Training on fixed-length segments meant context was severed at every segment boundary, and the model had to restart cold.
mechanism: Cache the hidden states of the previous segment and let the current segment attend to them (without backpropagating into them), plus a relative positional encoding that stays valid across the join.
buys: Effective context far longer than the training segment
Removes the hard boundary where context was previously thrown away
Much faster evaluation, since segments are not recomputed from scratch
costs: Cached states are stale — produced by older weights during training, and never receive gradient
Memory grows with the cached segment, which is the KV-cache problem in an early form
The recurrence over segments reintroduces a sequential dependency
pick_when: Superseded, but its cached-state idea is the direct ancestor of both the modern KV cache and sliding-window attention.

name: Sparse attention (strided / fixed patterns)
title_check: Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers
plain: Do not let every word look at every word. Let it look at its neighbours plus every few words, so news still travels in two hops, but a human draws that pattern in advance and it cannot know which word actually mattered.
problem: O(n²) made long sequences — images, audio, long documents — simply unaffordable.
mechanism: Do not let every token attend to every token. Use a fixed hand-designed pattern: each token attends to a local neighbourhood plus every k-th token, so information can still route globally in two hops.
buys: Drops cost to O(n√n), which made tens of thousands of tokens tractable for the first time
Keeps exact softmax over the tokens it does look at — no approximation of the attention function itself
Two-hop routing means distant tokens remain reachable
costs: The pattern is chosen by a human in advance and is completely content-blind — it cannot know which token actually mattered
Information between distant tokens must route through intermediaries, so it is lossy compared to full attention
Needs custom kernels to realise the theoretical saving; a naive implementation is slower than dense
If the important token is not on your stride, you never see it
pick_when: Rarely by itself now — learned sparsity (NSA, MoBA, DSA) beats fixed patterns. Still the right mental model for what all sparse attention is doing.

name: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)
title_check: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need
plain: All the question-askers share one single set of labels instead of each keeping their own. Memory drops enormously and quality drops noticeably, because the askers are now forced to agree on what to look for.
problem: Generating one token at a time is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound: you reload the entire KV cache from memory for every single token. With MHA that cache is multiplied by the head count.
mechanism: Keep all the query heads, but give them a single shared key head and a single shared value head. The cache shrinks by a factor equal to the number of heads.
math_note: Definitional arithmetic, and the same expression the calculator on this page evaluates. One shared K/V head instead of h of them.
buys: Cuts KV cache by the full head count — typically 8–64× less memory
Decoding speeds up dramatically because far less data crosses the memory bus per token
Query heads still differ, so some multi-head expressiveness survives
costs: Measurable quality loss versus MHA, and training can become less stable
All heads are forced to agree on what to retrieve, which is exactly the diversity multi-head attention existed to provide
Converting an MHA checkpoint to MQA requires retraining or uptraining
pick_when: When memory bandwidth is the hard limit and you can afford some quality: very high-throughput serving, or small models where the cache dominates. Most systems now choose GQA instead, as a better point on the same curve.
confused_with: Proposed in November 2019 and then largely ignored until around 2023. 'Launched' and 'mattered' are four years apart — the KV-cache bill was not yet due.

name: Sliding-window + global attention (Longformer)
title_check: Longformer: The Long-Document Transformer
plain: Each word looks only at a window of nearby words, plus a handful of special words that everyone can see. The cost stops growing quadratically, but anything outside the window is simply invisible in that layer.
problem: Document-level tasks needed thousands of tokens, but BERT-style models capped at 512.
mechanism: Each token attends to a fixed window of w neighbours, giving O(n·w) cost. A handful of designated tokens (like [CLS]) attend globally and are attended to by everyone, providing a routing hub.
buys: Linear in sequence length for a fixed window
Stacking layers grows the receptive field, so layer L sees roughly L·w tokens
The global tokens give an explicit escape hatch for information that must travel far in one hop
costs: Anything outside the window is invisible in that layer — genuine information loss, not approximation
Which tokens get to be global is a human design decision, made before seeing the data
Needs custom kernels to be fast
Long-range dependencies must survive multiple hops of averaging
pick_when: Long documents with mostly-local structure and a few known anchor points. The window idea survives into modern hybrids; the hand-picked global tokens mostly did not.
confused_with: Sliding-window attention is frequently attributed to Mistral (2023). Mistral productionised it in a major LLM; the mechanism is from here and from Sparse Transformers before it.

name: Linformer (low-rank projection)
title_check: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
authors: Wang, Li, Khabsa, Fang, Ma (Facebook AI)
plain: Squash the sequence down to a fixed number of rows before matching, on the theory that the attention pattern is simpler than it looks. It cannot be used for generating text one word at a time, which is why it did not last.
problem: If the attention matrix is empirically low-rank, paying for all n² entries is waste.
mechanism: Project the length-n key and value sequences down to a fixed k rows with a learned linear map, then attend against those k. Cost becomes O(n·k), linear in n.
buys: Genuinely linear in sequence length
Simple to implement — two extra projection matrices, no custom kernels
Backed by an empirical observation that attention matrices really are close to low-rank
costs: The projection is over the *sequence* dimension, so it bakes in a fixed maximum length — it does not generalise to longer inputs
Incompatible with causal decoding, which rules out autoregressive generation
The low-rank assumption fails exactly on retrieval-style tasks where one specific distant token matters
pick_when: Effectively obsolete, and instructive: it is the clearest example of a method that wins on complexity class and loses on applicability.

name: Linear attention (kernel / associativity trick)
title_check: Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention
plain: Drop the softmax and the arithmetic rearranges so you keep one fixed-size summary instead of a table that grows with every word. Memory stops growing entirely; what you lose is the ability to reach back and pick out one specific earlier word.
problem: The softmax is what forces you to build the full n×n matrix. Remove it and matrix multiplication becomes reassociable.
mechanism: Replace exp(qᵀk) with a feature map φ(q)ᵀφ(k). Now (φ(Q)φ(K)ᵀ)V can be reassociated as φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV), so you accumulate a fixed-size d×d state instead of an n×n matrix. Autoregressively this is literally an RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state.
math:
S_t = S_{t−1} + v_t k_tᵀ          (state, fixed size)
o_t = S_t q_t
math_note: Essential form, written in the same convention as the delta-rule entries so the family can be compared line by line. A feature map φ is applied to q and k; the point here is that the update only ever adds, so nothing is removed.
buys: O(n) time and O(1) memory in sequence length — the state is the same size at 1K tokens and at 1M
No KV cache at all: the state replaces it
Constant-time per generated token, so decoding does not slow down as context grows
costs: Loses everything softmax provided: guaranteed-positive weights, sum-to-one normalisation, competition between tokens, and a fresh distribution per query. Every query now reads the same accumulated state
The fixed state is a hard information bottleneck — recall of a specific distant token degrades badly, which is why pure linear models lose on retrieval
The naive update only *adds* to the state, so old contributions are never removed — the exact failure the delta rule was invented to fix
Quality gap versus softmax attention that took roughly four more years of work to start closing
pick_when: Never pure, in 2025+. As one layer type in a hybrid stack — three linear layers per exact layer — it is excellent. The fixed state is what buys you million-token contexts.

name: BigBird (local + global + random)
title_check: Big Bird: Transformers for Longer Sequences
authors: Zaheer, Guruganesh, Dubey, Ainslie, Alberti, Ontanon, et al. (Google)
plain: Local windows, a few globally visible words, and some random connections, which together come with a proof that nothing important becomes unreachable. Random jumps are slow on a graphics card, and the proof needs more layers than anyone actually uses.
problem: Sparse patterns worked, but was there any guarantee they preserved what full attention could compute?
mechanism: Combine three patterns: local windows, a few global tokens, and a set of random connections. The random edges turn the attention graph into an expander, which yields a theoretical guarantee.
buys: Linear complexity with a proof that it is a universal sequence-function approximator and Turing-complete
Random edges keep the graph diameter small, so information routes in few hops
Strong results on long-document QA and summarisation
costs: The theory requires a number of layers that the practical configurations do not use, so the guarantee is weaker than it sounds
Random access patterns are hostile to GPU memory coalescing — poor hardware utilisation
Three overlaid patterns make it fiddly to implement and tune
pick_when: Mostly of theoretical interest now. Its lesson — that you need *some* long-range escape hatch, not just local windows — is what modern hybrids encode by keeping full-attention layers.

name: Performer (FAVOR+ random features)
title_check: Rethinking Attention with Performers
authors: Choromanski, Likhosherstov, Dohan, Song, Gane, Sarlos, et al. (Google)
plain: Approximate the softmax itself using random features, so the cost becomes proportional to length rather than length squared. It is an estimate, so it is noisy, and damping the noise costs back the speed you saved.
problem: Linear attention's arbitrary feature map is not the softmax. Could you approximate the actual softmax kernel and keep linear cost?
mechanism: Approximate exp(qᵀk) with positive orthogonal random features, so the softmax kernel itself is estimated in a linear-cost form with provable error bounds.
buys: Linear cost while genuinely approximating softmax, not replacing it with something else
Unbiased estimate with concentration guarantees
Can be swapped into a pretrained softmax model with some finetuning
costs: It is an estimator — variance shows up as noise, and you need many random features to keep it low, which erodes the speed advantage
Empirically loses to exact attention on recall-heavy tasks
Made largely moot by FlashAttention, which delivered exact attention at speeds the approximations could not beat
pick_when: Rarely. Its historical role is as the high-water mark of the approximation era, right before exactness won.

name: The delta rule (fast weight programmers)
title_check: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
plain: If a memory slot holds 40 and the model now wants it to be 55, plain linear attention adds and gets 95. This reads the slot first and writes only the difference, so it lands on 55 and the memory gets reused instead of silting up.
problem: Linear attention's state update only ever adds. If the state holds 40 for some key and the model now wants 55, adding gives 95. The old value is never removed, and the fixed-size state saturates with stale content.
mechanism: Before writing, read out what the state currently holds for this key. Compute the difference between what is wanted and what is there, and write only that difference. The state is edited rather than accumulated — a genuine write, not an append.
math:
S_t = S_{t−1}( I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ ) + β_t v_t k_tᵀ
o_t = S_t q_t
math_note: Verbatim from the Gated DeltaNet paper. Read it against the line above: the ( I − β k kᵀ ) factor is what erases the old value for this key before the new one is written, instead of piling on top of it.
buys: Fixes the saturation problem: capacity is reused instead of being consumed monotonically
Substantially better associative recall than plain linear attention at the same state size
Reframes linear attention as a network writing to its own fast weights, which is what made the later work possible
costs: The read-before-write makes the recurrence harder to parallelise, which held it back for three years until the 2024 chunked algorithm
Still a fixed-size state, so it is still a bottleneck — better bookkeeping, not more capacity
No forgetting mechanism yet: it can overwrite a slot, but not decide to let a memory decay
pick_when: As the foundation of the modern linear-attention family. On its own, superseded by Gated DeltaNet.
confused_with: The delta rule idea is from 2021; the *parallelisable* DeltaNet that made it practical is 2024 (arXiv 2406.06484). Class described it as 'that paper came out in 2024', which is right for the parallel formulation.

name: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
title_check: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
authors: Su, Lu, Pan, Murtadha, Wen, Liu
plain: Rotate each word's question and label by an angle set by its position. Because a comparison only ever sees the difference between two angles, the model gets distance for free, with no extra table and no extra parameters.
problem: Additive position vectors are absolute, must survive every layer, and cannot extrapolate. Relative schemes worked better but cost a per-pair tensor.
mechanism: Take Q and K in 2D pairs of dimensions and rotate each pair by an angle proportional to its position, with a different frequency per pair. Because a dot product between two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of their angles, the attention score automatically depends on *relative* distance — with no extra tensor and no extra parameters.
math: ⟨ R_Θ,m q , R_Θ,n k ⟩ = ⟨ q , R_Θ,(n−m) k ⟩
math_note: The defining identity, in essential form. Rotating a query at position m and a key at position n gives an inner product that depends only on n − m, which is how relative position appears without any extra tensor.
buys: Relative position falls out of the geometry for free — shift both tokens and the score is unchanged
Zero parameters, and applied directly to Q and K inside attention rather than added at the input, so it cannot be washed out
Defined at any position, so nothing runs off the end of a table
Compatible with FlashAttention and with KV caching, which is a large part of why it won
costs: Extrapolation degrades well before the maths breaks: high-frequency dimensions have wrapped many times by the tens of thousands of tokens, and long-range discrimination gets weak
The base frequency is a hyperparameter you are committing to at pretraining time — changing it later requires rescaling tricks or finetuning
Applies only to Q and K, so V carries no positional information
Long-range decay is an empirical tendency, not a guarantee like ALiBi's
pick_when: The default for essentially every modern LLM. If you intend to extend context later, pretrain with a large base frequency, or plan for YaRN — or plan to drop it entirely (see DroPE).

name: Top-k attention
title_check: Memory-efficient Transformers via Top-k Attention
plain: Keep only the handful of best-matching words for each question and ignore the rest, since most of the attention was near zero anyway. But you still have to score everything before you can tell which are best, so it saves memory rather than work.
problem: Softmax attention is already nearly sparse in practice — most weights are close to zero. Why pay to compute and store all of them?
mechanism: Keep only the k highest-scoring keys per query and softmax over just those. Unlike fixed patterns, which tokens survive is decided by content, per query, at runtime.
math: o_i = Σ_{j ∈ TopK_k(q_i·k_j)}  softmax_j( q_i·k_j / √d ) v_j
math_note: Essential form. Note what the notation hides: TopK needs every q_i·k_j scored before it can rank them, which is why this saves memory rather than work.
buys: Content-adaptive rather than hand-drawn — it keeps what actually scored highly
A good approximation of full attention precisely because attention really is near-sparse
Big memory savings, and usable as a drop-in at inference on an already-trained model
costs: You must compute all the scores before you can rank them, so the naive version saves memory but not the O(n²) score computation — this is why NSA and DSA later add a cheap indexer to avoid scoring everything
Top-k selection is a sort, which is not GPU-friendly and does not fuse cleanly into FlashAttention-style kernels
Hard truncation discards the tail of the distribution; when many tokens matter weakly, that tail was real signal
Applied only at inference it creates a train/test mismatch
pick_when: As a concept it is the direct ancestor of every learned-sparsity method that followed. In its 2021 form, superseded by NSA/MoBA/DSA, which make the selection cheap and trainable.

name: ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases)
title_check: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation
plain: Do not encode position at all. Just subtract a penalty that grows with distance so nearby words win, which keeps working far past the trained length but permanently biases the model against anything far away.
problem: Every positional scheme so far degraded when tested past its training length. Could you train on 1K tokens and actually run on 2K?
mechanism: Do not encode position at all. Just subtract a penalty proportional to the distance between query and key from the attention score, with a different fixed slope per head. Near tokens are favoured; far tokens are damped, smoothly and without limit.
math_note: Verbatim from the paper. The head-specific slopes m form a geometric sequence starting at 2^(−8/n) with that same value as the ratio, for n heads.
buys: Genuinely extrapolates — train short, test long, which was the paper's whole claim and it holds
Zero parameters, and almost zero compute: one bias added to the scores
Trivial to implement
The distance penalty is monotone by construction, so behaviour past the training length is predictable rather than merely undefined
costs: Hard-codes a recency prior. Any task needing a token from the distant past fights the bias, and long-range retrieval measurably suffers
The per-head slopes are fixed by hand, not learned
Its extrapolation is partly the effect of an implicit local window — it stays coherent at length rather than genuinely using the far context
Largely lost to RoPE in practice, because RoPE plus a rescaling trick reaches longer contexts with better long-range recall
pick_when: When you need graceful behaviour past the training length with no finetuning and your task is locality-dominated. For long-context retrieval, RoPE with YaRN beats it.

name: FlashAttention (IO-aware exact attention)
title_check: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
plain: Never write the giant score table out to slow memory. Compute it in tiles inside the chip's fast memory instead, giving an identical answer, and this pure engineering made exact attention faster than most of the clever approximations.
problem: Everyone had been attacking attention's FLOP count. But attention was never compute-bound — it was bound by moving the n×n matrix to and from GPU high-bandwidth memory.
mechanism: Never materialise the attention matrix. Tile Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, and compute softmax incrementally across tiles using the online-softmax trick. The result is bit-for-bit exact attention with O(n) memory traffic.
math:
m⁽ʲ⁾ = max( m⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾ , rowmax(S⁽ʲ⁾) )
ℓ⁽ʲ⁾ = e^( m⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾ − m⁽ʲ⁾ ) ℓ⁽ʲ⁻¹⁾ + rowsum( e^( S⁽ʲ⁾ − m⁽ʲ⁾ ) )
math_note: Essential form: the online-softmax recurrence that lets a softmax be computed tile by tile without ever holding the full n×n matrix. The running max and sum are rescaled as each new tile arrives, which is why the result is exact rather than approximate.
buys: Exact — no approximation whatsoever, unlike everything else in this era
2–4× faster in wall-clock time and dramatically less memory, enabling much longer contexts with no modelling change
A pure drop-in: no retraining, no architecture change, no quality cost
Reframed the entire field around memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs
costs: Still O(n²) in arithmetic — it changes the constant and the memory, not the complexity class, so it postpones the wall rather than removing it
Hardware-specific hand-written kernels, needing a rewrite per GPU generation
Fusing anything custom into attention (odd masks, bespoke biases) became much harder — a real constraint on what mechanisms are practical
pick_when: Always. There is no reason to run unfused attention in 2026. Its deeper significance is strategic: it made exact attention fast enough that most approximate methods stopped being worth their quality cost.

name: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)
title_check: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
authors: Ainslie, Lee-Thorp, de Jong, Zemlyanskiy, Lebrón, Sanghai (Google)
plain: A middle setting between every asker having its own labels and all of them sharing one: split the askers into groups with one set of labels each. Most of the memory saving for a small fraction of the quality loss, which is why it became the default.
problem: MHA's KV cache is unaffordable to serve; MQA's single shared head costs too much quality. The gap between them was unexplored.
mechanism: Interpolate. Split the query heads into g groups and give each group its own shared K and V. g = heads is MHA; g = 1 is MQA; g = 8 with 64 query heads is the usual sweet spot. Existing MHA checkpoints can be converted by mean-pooling the K/V heads within each group and uptraining briefly.
math: cache_bytes = 2 · L · (h / g) · d_head · T · b
math_note: Definitional. g = 1 recovers MHA; g = h recovers MQA. The whole method is that middle term being a dial rather than a choice of two.
buys: Most of MQA's memory saving with most of MHA's quality — an unusually favourable trade
A dial, not a binary choice: pick g to fit your memory budget
Converts existing MHA checkpoints cheaply, so nobody had to retrain from scratch
Maps naturally onto tensor parallelism, with one KV group per device
costs: Still a real quality loss versus true MHA, just a smaller one
The cache still grows linearly with sequence length and with concurrent users — it reduces the constant, it does not change the shape of the problem
g is another hyperparameter to tune, and the best value is model- and workload-dependent
Superseded on pure memory grounds by MLA, which compresses instead of sharing
pick_when: The default for production serving, and the correct baseline. For a 2K chatbot the saving is nice; at 128K with many concurrent users it is the difference between shipping and not. Choose MLA instead if you are designing a new model and can afford the added complexity.
confused_with: Not the same as GSA (Gated Slot Attention). Similar acronym, unrelated mechanism, different category entirely.

name: RWKV
title_check: RWKV: Reinventing RNNs for the Transformer Era
authors: Peng, Alcaide, Anthony, Albalak, Arcadinho, et al.
plain: Train it in parallel like a Transformer, then run it as a loop with fixed memory like an old-fashioned recurrent network. Nothing grows as the conversation gets longer, but fixed memory limits how well it recalls one specific distant fact.
problem: Transformers parallelise but cost O(n²) and a growing cache; RNNs are O(n) with constant memory but cannot be parallelised across time.
mechanism: A linear-attention-family architecture with a time-decay weighting that can be written as a parallel form for training and an exactly equivalent recurrent form for inference.
buys: Trains in parallel like a Transformer, runs as an RNN with constant memory per token
No KV cache at all, so serving memory is flat in context length
Demonstrated at genuine LLM scale, which most linear models had not managed
costs: The fixed state bottlenecks long-range recall, the standing weakness of the whole family
The time decay imposes a recency prior similar in spirit to ALiBi's
A smaller ecosystem, so tooling and kernels lag the mainstream
pick_when: Memory-constrained or edge deployment where flat inference memory matters more than peak recall. Its ideas now mostly appear inside hybrids.

name: NoPE (no positional encoding)
title_check: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
authors: Kazemnejad, Padhi, Natesan Ramamurthy, Das, Reddy
plain: In a text generator each word can already tell how many words came before it, so position may not need encoding at all. It stretches to longer inputs well, but the trick only works in this one-directional setting.
problem: Every positional scheme has extrapolation failures. What if a causal decoder does not need an explicit one at all?
mechanism: Remove positional encoding entirely from a decoder-only model. The causal mask already breaks permutation symmetry — a token can count how many tokens precede it — so the model can learn position implicitly.
buys: Length-generalises better than the explicit schemes it was compared against
Zero parameters and zero compute
Shows the implicit positional signal in the causal mask is real and usable
costs: Only works for decoder-only causal models; an encoder has no such signal
Results were established at modest scale, and behaviour at frontier scale is a different question
Explicit position still helps convergence early in training, so dropping it from the start costs you something
pick_when: Not as a from-scratch choice for a large model. Its importance is that it makes DroPE's premise credible: if the model can encode position without RoPE, you can train with RoPE and then take it away.

name: Positional Interpolation (PI)
title_check: Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation
plain: Instead of asking the model to handle position 8000 that it has never seen, relabel it as position 2000 that it has. Everything stays in familiar territory, but squeezing all the positions together blurs the difference between neighbouring words.
problem: RoPE models break past their trained length because the rotation angles go out of distribution. Retraining at longer context is prohibitively expensive.
mechanism: Do not extrapolate — interpolate. Divide every position index by a scale factor so that position 8000 in a 2048-trained model is presented as position 2000. All angles stay inside the trained range. A short finetune adapts the model.
math: f′(x, m) = f( x , m · L / L′ )
math_note: Essential form. Position m in the extended window L′ is presented to the model as the position it would have occupied in the original window L.
buys: Extends context many-fold with roughly a thousand finetuning steps instead of a full retrain
Stays strictly inside the distribution the model already knows, which is why it is stable
Simple: one divisor
costs: Squashes all frequencies equally, including the high-frequency dimensions that encode fine local distance — adjacent tokens become harder to tell apart, and short-context performance measurably degrades
Requires finetuning; it is not zero-shot
The scale factor caps your extension: you must choose the target length up front
pick_when: Superseded by NTK-aware scaling and YaRN, which fix the uniform-squashing flaw. Still the conceptual root of every RoPE-rescaling method.

name: NTK-aware scaled RoPE
date_evidence: Reddit post by u/bloc97 in r/LocalLLaMA (thread 14lz7j5), late June 2023. Corroborated by huggingface/text-generation-inference issue #512, opened July 2023. This method has no arXiv paper; it was never formally published as a standalone work, and was later folded into the YaRN paper.
plain: Squeeze the slow-moving parts of the position signal and leave the fast-moving parts alone, so nearby words stay easy to tell apart. It needs no retraining at all, which is why it spread within days, but it was a good hunch rather than a derived result.
problem: Positional Interpolation squashes every RoPE frequency by the same factor, destroying the high-frequency dimensions that distinguish nearby tokens. Result: longer context, worse local resolution.
mechanism: Scale frequencies unevenly instead. Change the RoPE base so that low-frequency dimensions (which encode long-range position and have not wrapped) are interpolated, while high-frequency dimensions (which encode local distance) are left nearly untouched. Spend the distortion where it does least damage.
math_note: Essential form, and this method has no paper - see the date evidence. Changing the base rather than the positions scales the frequencies unevenly, which is exactly the point: the fast-turning dimensions are left almost untouched.
buys: Works with no finetuning at all, unlike PI — this is why it spread through the community within days
Preserves short-range resolution, so local quality holds up far better than PI
One line of code: change the base
costs: Zero-shot quality still degrades at large extension factors; it stretches further than PI but not indefinitely
The frequency split is heuristic, not derived — YaRN's contribution was making it principled
It also scales frequencies that did not need scaling, which YaRN later corrects with explicit wavelength-based ramping
No peer review, no formal evaluation at the time of release
pick_when: As a zero-shot emergency extension of an existing RoPE model. If you can finetune at all, use YaRN, which dominates it on every axis.
confused_with: There is no NTK-aware scaling *paper*. Any citation with an arXiv ID for this method is citing something that does not exist — the canonical sources are a Reddit post and a GitHub issue. The name references Neural Tangent Kernel theory by analogy; it is not a result derived from NTK theory.

name: FlashAttention-2
title_check: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
plain: The same exact-attention trick, rewritten to keep the graphics card busier. About twice as fast, and still identical down to the last digit.
problem: FlashAttention reached only about 25–40% of the GPU's theoretical peak, because of how work was split across thread blocks and warps.
mechanism: Rework the parallelisation: fewer non-matmul operations, parallelise over sequence length as well as batch and heads, and partition work between warps to cut shared-memory traffic.
buys: Roughly 2× faster than FlashAttention, reaching 50–73% of peak
Still bit-for-bit exact
Another pure drop-in
costs: Still O(n²) arithmetic
Tuned for Ampere/Hopper; older hardware sees less benefit
Deepens the ecosystem's dependence on a small number of hand-written kernels
pick_when: The practical default on NVIDIA hardware before Hopper-specific FA3.

name: RetNet (retention)
title_check: Retentive Network: A Successor to Transformer for Large Language Models
plain: Write the same model three different ways: as a parallel one for training, as a loop for generating, and as a chunked one for very long inputs. You get fast training and constant-memory generation from one architecture - but what it forgets is decided by a fixed rule rather than learned.
problem: Linear-attention models forced a choice: train in parallel like a Transformer, or decode cheaply like an RNN. Nobody had one architecture that genuinely did both without a separate implementation for each.
mechanism: Replace attention with retention, which the paper derives as the connection between recurrence and attention, and which admits three mathematically equivalent forms: a parallel representation for training, a recurrent one giving O(1) inference, and a chunkwise recurrent one that encodes each chunk in parallel while summarising chunks recurrently for linear-complexity long-sequence work.
buys: One architecture with three equivalent computation forms - the cleanest statement of that idea anyone had made
O(1) decoding memory and cost, improving throughput and latency without a quality penalty at the scales tested
The chunkwise form handles long sequences in linear complexity, so long context does not force a different implementation
Trains in parallel, unlike a true RNN
costs: The decay is data-independent - a fixed gamma per head or layer, so the model cannot decide what to forget based on what it is reading. Mamba, GLA and Gated DeltaNet all beat it precisely by making that gate learned and content-dependent
Fixed-size state, so the recall ceiling of the whole linear family applies unchanged
The paper's framing as a 'successor to Transformer' did not hold: no frontier model replaced attention with retention, and the field went to hybrids instead
Tooling and ecosystem never approached the Transformer's, which compounds the adoption problem
pick_when: Rarely as a deployment choice now. It belongs on this timeline as the clearest articulation of parallel-train / recurrent-decode duality, an idea that everything from Mamba-2 to Gated DeltaNet later built on with a learned gate instead of a fixed one.
confused_with: Retention is not attention with a decay bolted on - the paper derives it from the recurrence/attention connection. But its fixed decay is exactly the thing later linear models replaced, which is the reason it reads as a stepping stone rather than a successor.

name: YaRN (Yet another RoPE extensioN)
title_check: YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models
plain: Work out which parts of the position signal have already wrapped around and stretch only those, plus a correction for how stretching changes the model's confidence. The best of the stretching methods, though it still works best with a short retraining.
problem: PI squashed all frequencies; NTK-aware fixed that with a heuristic. Neither had a principled account of *which* frequencies to touch, and both lost accuracy at high extension factors.
mechanism: Split RoPE dimensions by wavelength relative to context length. Dimensions whose wavelength is much shorter than the context are left alone (they encode local distance); dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the context are interpolated; in between, ramp smoothly. Add a temperature adjustment to the attention logits to correct the entropy shift that stretching causes.
buys: State of the art among RoPE rescaling methods — extends further with less degradation than PI or NTK-aware
Needs roughly 10× fewer tokens and 2.5× fewer steps of finetuning than PI
The wavelength criterion is principled rather than a tuned heuristic
The logit temperature fix is a real insight: stretching positions changes attention entropy, and correcting it matters
Works zero-shot in a degraded 'Dynamic-YaRN' form too
costs: Still fundamentally a patch on a model that was pretrained short — it does not match a model natively trained long
Best results need finetuning, so it is not free
More hyperparameters than PI: ramp boundaries and temperature
Extension factors much beyond ~32× still degrade; it moves the wall rather than removing it
pick_when: The right choice for extending an existing RoPE model's context — the standard tool, used in many open-weight long-context releases. If you are training a new model, prefer a large RoPE base from the start, or consider dropping positional encoding entirely.
confused_with: Routinely cited as September 2023. The arXiv v1 is 31 August 2023.

name: PagedAttention (vLLM)
title_check: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
authors: Kwon, Li, Zhuang, Sheng, Zheng, Yu, Gonzalez, Zhang, Stoica
plain: The problem was not how big the stored memory was but how much of it was wasted, since reserving one large block per user threw most of it away. Borrowing the operating system's paging idea reclaims the gaps and multiplies throughput without touching the model at all.
problem: Not the size of the KV cache but its *management*: reserving one contiguous slab per request wasted 60–80% of it to internal fragmentation and over-reservation.
mechanism: Borrow virtual memory paging. Store the cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks with a lookup table, so memory is allocated on demand and identical prefixes can be shared copy-on-write across requests.
buys: 2–4× throughput improvement purely from better memory management — no model change at all
Near-zero fragmentation waste
Prefix sharing makes multi-sample generation and shared system prompts dramatically cheaper
costs: Indirection through a block table adds a small per-access overhead
Significant serving-system complexity
Solves waste, not growth — the cache still scales with tokens and users
pick_when: Any production serving stack. Included here because 'reduce the KV cache' and 'stop wasting the KV cache' are different problems, and the second one was worth as much as several architectural tricks.

name: Attention sinks (StreamingLLM)
title_check: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
plain: A model has to spread exactly 100% of its attention somewhere, so when it wants nothing it dumps the leftovers on the first few words. Delete those and everything falls apart, so keep them forever: four words of memory buys unlimited streaming.
problem: A naive sliding-window cache should let a model stream forever. In practice, the moment the very first tokens are evicted, perplexity explodes. Nobody knew why.
mechanism: The diagnosis is the contribution: softmax must sum to one, so when a query has nothing it genuinely wants, it dumps probability mass on the first few tokens regardless of content. Those tokens are 'sinks'. Evict them and every attention distribution is forced to renormalise onto tokens it never wanted. The fix is to permanently keep the first ~4 tokens' KV alongside the sliding window.
math_note: Essential form. The first s tokens are pinned permanently alongside the rolling window of w. Typically s = 4, which is the entire cost of the method.
buys: Enables genuinely unbounded streaming with constant memory — millions of tokens without a perplexity blowup
Costs 4 tokens of cache. The cheapest fix on this entire timeline relative to what it enables
No finetuning, no architecture change; applies to already-trained models
Explains a real and previously mysterious failure mode, which is why the insight spread so fast
costs: Does not extend context — the model still cannot *use* information outside its window. It stays fluent, it does not become long-context
Anything evicted is gone permanently, so it is unsuitable for retrieval over the full history
A workaround for an artefact of softmax normalisation, rather than a fix to the underlying cause
Later work addresses the root cause directly at pretraining time by letting attention weights not sum to one
pick_when: Long-running chat or streaming where you need bounded memory and coherence, and you accept a bounded effective context. Combine with sliding windows. Do not reach for it if the task needs recall over the whole history.

name: Ring Attention
title_check: Ring Attention with Blockwise Transformers for Near-Infinite Context
plain: Split one very long sequence across many graphics cards arranged in a ring and pass the pieces around while they compute. Context grows with the number of machines you own; the total amount of work is unchanged.
problem: Even with FlashAttention, one device's memory caps context length. The limit had become the device, not the algorithm.
mechanism: Shard the sequence across devices in a ring. Each device holds a block of Q and rotates K/V blocks around the ring, overlapping communication with computation so the transfer is effectively free.
buys: Context scales linearly with device count — no per-device length limit
Exact attention, no approximation
Communication hides behind computation when block sizes are chosen well
costs: Needs a multi-device cluster with fast interconnect; useless on one GPU
Total FLOPs are unchanged and still quadratic — it distributes the cost, it does not reduce it
Causal masking makes the ring's work unbalanced, needing careful scheduling
Interconnect bandwidth becomes the new bottleneck
pick_when: Training or inference at very long context on a cluster you already own. It is a systems answer to a systems problem, and composes with everything else here.

name: Sliding-window attention in production (Mistral 7B)
title_check: Mistral 7B
authors: Jiang, Sablayrolles, Mensch, Bamford, Chaplot, et al. (Mistral AI)
plain: Every layer looks only at the last few thousand words, but stacking layers lets information travel much further, one hop at a time. Memory stops growing, at the price of being noticeably worse at fetching one exact fact from far back.
problem: Sliding windows had existed since 2019 but were seen as an encoder trick for long documents. Could a frontier decoder-only LLM just use one everywhere?
mechanism: Every layer attends only to the previous w tokens (w = 4096). Because the receptive field compounds with depth, a 32-layer stack reaches roughly 131K tokens of theoretical context while the KV cache is capped at w per layer, enabling a rolling buffer cache.
buys: KV cache is bounded by the window, not by context length — a fixed memory ceiling regardless of how long the conversation runs
Compounding receptive field means real long-range information can still propagate, layer by layer
Cheap enough that a 7B model outperformed a 13B on many benchmarks
Combines naturally with a rolling buffer and with attention sinks
costs: Multi-hop propagation is lossy: information reaches distant tokens only after being averaged through intermediate layers, so it is nothing like true long-range attention
Retrieval of a specific distant fact is markedly worse than full attention — the classic needle-in-a-haystack weakness
The window is fixed at training time
Naive implementations break badly without attention sinks once eviction starts
pick_when: Excellent for conversational workloads with bounded memory and mostly-local dependencies. Wrong on its own for long-document retrieval or agents needing precise recall — which is why current models interleave windowed and full-attention layers rather than using windows everywhere.
confused_with: Mistral is frequently credited with inventing sliding-window attention. It productionised it at scale; the mechanism dates to Sparse Transformers (2019) and Longformer (2020).

name: Mamba (selective state space model)
title_check: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
plain: A different design altogether: a loop with fixed-size memory that decides, based on what it is reading, what to keep and what to drop. Fast and constant-memory, but weaker than attention when it has to copy an exact detail.
problem: Earlier state-space models were linear-time but content-blind: their dynamics were fixed, so they could not choose what to remember based on what they were reading.
mechanism: Make the SSM parameters functions of the input, so the model can selectively propagate or forget. This breaks the convolutional formulation, so it is paired with a hardware-aware parallel scan that keeps the state in fast memory.
buys: Linear time, constant inference memory, ~5× higher decoding throughput than a Transformer of similar size
Selectivity closes much of the gap to attention on content-dependent tasks
Genuinely competitive quality at small and mid scale
costs: Fixed-size state means the recall ceiling of the whole linear family still applies — it loses on exact copying and retrieval
In-context learning is weaker than attention, in ways that matter for few-shot prompting
The parallel scan needs a bespoke kernel
Pure Mamba has largely given way to hybrids, which is the honest verdict on it
pick_when: As the recurrent half of a hybrid stack. Included because it is the most prominent non-attention challenger, and because its outcome — absorbed into hybrids rather than replacing attention — is the pattern the whole linear family follows.

name: Gated Linear Attention (GLA)
title_check: Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training
plain: Add a learned forget dial to linear attention so old memories fade on purpose instead of piling up forever. Deciding what to forget turns out to matter about as much as deciding what to store.
problem: Linear attention's state accumulates forever with no way to forget, and the delta rule alone could overwrite a slot but not let memories decay.
mechanism: Add a data-dependent gate that decays the state at each step, so the model learns what to forget and how fast. Paired with a chunkwise-parallel algorithm that keeps training efficient on tensor cores.
buys: Learned forgetting, which turns out to matter as much as learned writing
Chunkwise-parallel training keeps it hardware-efficient
Clearly better than ungated linear attention at equal state size
costs: Still fixed-state, still recall-limited
Gating adds parameters and another thing to tune
Chunked training is significantly more complex to implement correctly
pick_when: As a building block. Its importance is that gating plus the delta rule is exactly the combination Gated DeltaNet lands on a year later.

name: Infini-attention
title_check: Leave No Context Behind: Efficient Infinite Context Transformers with Infini-attention
plain: Rather than throwing away words that drop out of the window, fold them into a compressed summary and keep that. The summary is lossy, and other groups have had mixed luck reproducing the results.
problem: Sliding windows throw away evicted tokens entirely. Could you keep a summary of them instead of nothing?
mechanism: Give each attention layer both a local window and a compressive memory: evicted KV states are folded into a fixed-size associative matrix rather than discarded, and a learned gate blends the local and memory read-outs.
buys: Bounded memory with some access to arbitrarily old context, rather than a hard cutoff
Reuses the standard KV states, so it slots into existing architectures
Reported strong results on very long retrieval benchmarks
costs: The compressive memory is fixed-size and lossy — old detail is genuinely destroyed, not merely displaced
Independent reproduction has been mixed, and it did not see broad adoption
The gate between local and compressed memory is another trained component that can fail quietly
pick_when: Rarely in practice. Included because 'compress what you evict' is a real and recurring idea, and because a technique with strong reported numbers and weak adoption is worth being honest about.

name: Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA)
title_check: DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model
plain: Instead of making the askers share labels, squash each word's labels and content into one small code and unpack it per asker when needed. Around 93% less memory than the standard scheme with no loss in quality, but it has to be designed in from the very start.
problem: GQA reduces the KV cache by making heads share, which costs quality because heads stop being different. Could you shrink the cache without taking away head diversity?
mechanism: Compress rather than share. Project keys and values down into a single low-rank latent vector per token and cache only that. At use time each head projects back up to its own full K and V, and the up-projection can be folded into the existing weight matrices so it is nearly free. RoPE needs a decoupled extra dimension, because rotation does not commute with the compression.
math_note: Definitional. No factor of 2 and no head count: MLA caches one low-rank latent of width d_c per token per layer, and reprojects each head's K and V at use time.
buys: Roughly 93% KV cache reduction versus MHA — far beyond what GQA achieves
Quality reported as equal to or better than full MHA, unlike GQA and MQA which both cost quality
Every head keeps its own effective K and V, so head diversity survives
Absorbing the up-projection into adjacent weights means little runtime overhead
costs: Substantially more complex than GQA — the RoPE incompatibility forces a decoupled rotary dimension, which is a genuine wart
Cannot be retrofitted to an existing MHA checkpoint the way GQA can; it is a pretraining-time architectural commitment
The low-rank latent is a bottleneck, and its rank is another thing to get right
Kernel support is thinner than for GQA, so realising the gains needs work
pick_when: When designing a new model where inference memory is a first-class constraint and you can afford the complexity — especially at long context or high concurrency. Stay with GQA if you are adapting an existing checkpoint or want maximum ecosystem support.
confused_with: 'MSA' in the spoken assignment brief is ambiguous between MLA and NSA. The lecture described DeepSeek block compression with an indexer, which matches NSA better; both are covered here in full.

name: xLSTM (extended LSTM)
title_check: xLSTM: Extended Long Short-Term Memory
plain: Take the 1990s LSTM, fix the two things that made it lose to Transformers, and scale it to billions of parameters. It competes on quality and scales better with length - and yet no frontier model has actually adopted it, which is worth noticing.
problem: LSTMs built the first language models and were then comprehensively beaten by parallelisable self-attention. The open question was whether they lost on fundamentals or on two fixable limitations.
mechanism: Two changes. Exponential gating with normalisation and stabilisation, and a modified memory: sLSTM with a scalar memory and new memory mixing, and mLSTM with a matrix memory and a covariance update rule that is fully parallelisable. Both are wrapped in residual blocks and stacked.
buys: Performs favourably against state-of-the-art Transformers and state-space models on both quality and scaling
mLSTM is fully parallelisable, removing the sequential training bottleneck that sank the original LSTM
Linear time complexity, so it scales better with context length than a dense Transformer
A 2026 scaling-law study reports xLSTM Pareto-dominating Transformers on loss for a given compute budget
costs: Only mLSTM is fully parallelisable - sLSTM's memory mixing is not, so the architecture is a mix of parallel and sequential parts rather than uniformly parallel
Fixed-size memory, so the recall ceiling that limits every recurrent model applies here too

Despite a favourable published scaling curve, no frontier production model has adopted it. A good curve that has not translated into deployment is a real result about the method, not an oversight to explain away
Small ecosystem: kernels, serving support and tooling all lag the Transformer stack by a wide margin
pick_when: Worth knowing rather than deploying. Its importance to this timeline is as evidence that the recurrent line was never fundamentally beaten - it was beaten on parallelism, and once that was fixed the gap largely closed. Whether that matters in practice is exactly what the missing adoption tells you.

name: Mamba-2 (state space duality)
title_check: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
plain: Shows that two separate research lines were describing the same thing, which lets the computation run on the graphics card's fast matrix hardware. Several times quicker, though the constraints that make the equivalence hold cost a little expressiveness.
problem: State-space models and linear attention had been developed by separate communities with separate vocabularies, and Mamba's scan could not use tensor cores well.
mechanism: Show that SSMs and a class of linear attention are two views of the same structured-matrix decomposition. That equivalence yields an algorithm expressible as matrix multiplications, so it runs on tensor cores.
math:
S_t = α_t S_{t−1} + v_t k_tᵀ
o_t = S_t q_t
math_note: Verbatim, as quoted in the Gated DeltaNet paper. Gating without the delta rule: it can fade the whole state, but cannot make a targeted correction.
buys: 2–8× faster than Mamba while matching quality
Unifies two research lines, so improvements transfer between them
Uses tensor cores properly instead of a bespoke scan
costs: Structural constraints needed for the duality make the state transition less expressive than Mamba's
Still fixed-state and still recall-limited
The theory is genuinely hard, raising the barrier to contributing
pick_when: Over Mamba where speed matters. Its real significance is theoretical: after this, 'linear attention' and 'SSM' are the same conversation — which is why Gated DeltaNet is described as an improvement to Mamba-2.

name: DeltaNet, parallelised over sequence length
title_check: Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length
plain: The delta rule had been known since 2021 but had to run one step at a time, so nobody could train it at scale. This restructures it so the steps can be done in blocks, which is the engineering that turned a good idea into a usable one.
problem: The delta rule had been known since 2021 and was clearly better than plain linear attention, but its read-before-write recurrence was sequential, so it could not be trained at scale.
mechanism: Reformulate the chain of rank-1 state updates using a WY representation, letting the recurrence be computed chunkwise with matrix multiplications instead of step by step.
buys: Makes the delta rule trainable at scale — this is the paper that turned a good idea into a usable one
Clearly outperforms Mamba and GLA on associative recall at comparable size
Chunked form maps onto tensor cores
costs: Still slower per step than plain linear attention — the delta rule is not free
Still fixed-state: better memory management, not more memory
No forgetting yet; that arrives with Gated DeltaNet six months later
The chunked algorithm is intricate and easy to get subtly wrong
pick_when: Superseded by Gated DeltaNet, which adds gating. This is the engineering step that made the whole modern linear-attention revival possible.
confused_with: This is most likely the paper meant by 'the delta net paper came out in 2024'. The delta rule idea itself is 2021 (arXiv 2102.11174).

name: FlashAttention-3
title_check: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
authors: Shah, Bikshandi, Zhang, Thakkar, Ramani, Dao
plain: The exact-attention kernel rewritten again for the newest graphics cards, overlapping its work and adding an 8-bit mode. The fastest yet, but only on that hardware, and the 8-bit path is no longer exact.
problem: FlashAttention-2 was tuned for Ampere and left Hopper's asynchronous units and FP8 support unused.
mechanism: Exploit Hopper specifics: warp-specialisation with asynchronous copy and tensor-core instructions, interleaving of matmul and softmax, and FP8 with incoherent processing to limit quantisation error.
buys: 1.5–2× faster than FA2 on H100, reaching up to ~75% utilisation; near 1.2 PFLOPs/s in FP8
FP8 error roughly 2.6× lower than naive quantisation
Still exact in the FP16 path
costs: Hopper-only; no benefit on older hardware
The FP8 path is genuinely lossy — 'exact' applies to the FP16 path
Deep coupling to one GPU generation, so it needs rewriting again next time
pick_when: On H100-class hardware. Its recurring lesson is that a large share of practical attention progress is kernel engineering, not new mathematics.

name: Gated Slot Attention (GSA)
title_check: Gated Slot Attention for Efficient Linear-Time Sequence Modeling
authors: Zhang, Yang, Zhu, Qin, Zhang, et al.
plain: Keep a small set of memory slots, read them through a softmax, and let the model forget the ones it no longer needs. Unusually good recall for how little it stores, and unusually cheap to convert an existing model into.
problem: Linear models with a large recurrent state are expensive; ones with a small state forget. And converting a pretrained Transformer into a linear model usually required heavy retraining.
mechanism: Keep a bounded set of memory slots, read from them through a softmax, and add GLA-style gating so slots can be forgotten adaptively. Structurally it is two GLA layers joined by a softmax, which keeps the state small while retaining softmax's competition.
buys: Strong recall for its state size — notably better than other linear models on recall-intensive tasks
Retaining softmax makes finetuning a pretrained Transformer into GSA much cheaper, which is a practical advantage no other linear method offers as cleanly
Smaller state than RetNet or GLA at comparable quality, so training and inference are both cheaper
costs: Still a bounded-memory model, so it does not match full attention on hard long-range retrieval
The slot count is a capacity ceiling chosen up front
More complex than plain gated linear attention
Less ecosystem support than GQA or Mamba
pick_when: As the recurrent layer type in a hybrid, especially when you want to convert an existing Transformer rather than pretrain from scratch. This is the mechanism taught in class that the assignment's required list leaves out.
confused_with: Not GQA. GSA is a linear-attention method with bounded memory slots; GQA is a KV-head-sharing scheme for softmax attention. The acronyms differ by one letter and the mechanisms have nothing in common.

name: Differential Transformer
title_check: Differential Transformer
authors: Ye, Dong, Xia, Sun, Zhu, Huang, Wei (Microsoft)
plain: Compute two attention patterns and subtract one from the other, so the noise common to both cancels out, much like noise-cancelling headphones. It sharpens what the model looks at rather than making it cheaper, which is a rarer kind of improvement.
problem: Transformers allocate real attention mass to irrelevant context — 'attention noise' — which drowns the signal in long inputs and is part of why long-context retrieval degrades.
mechanism: Compute two separate softmax attention maps and subtract one from the other, scaled by a learned coefficient. Common-mode noise cancels the way it does in a differential amplifier, leaving a sparser and better-targeted pattern.
math_note: Essential form. Two attention maps, subtracted, so whatever noise is common to both cancels. λ is learned per layer.
buys: Measurably better long-context retrieval and less distraction by irrelevant context
Reduces activation outliers, which helps quantisation
Reaches comparable quality with roughly 65% of the parameters or training tokens
A rare genuinely new idea about the attention function itself, not about its cost
costs: Two attention maps means more compute per layer, though the maps are half-width so the overhead is modest
Adds a learned differential coefficient per layer
Not yet adopted at frontier scale, so the evidence base is thinner than for GQA or MLA
The KV cache cost is unchanged — this improves quality, not memory
pick_when: Worth considering when long-context retrieval quality is the binding constraint rather than memory. Included because almost everything else on this timeline makes attention cheaper; this one makes it *better*, which is a different and rarer kind of contribution.

name: Gated DeltaNet
title_check: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
plain: Combine a forget dial with the delta rule, so the model can both wipe things broadly and correct one detail precisely. It is the strongest of the fixed-memory family, and is still deployed alongside full attention rather than replacing it.
problem: Gating (Mamba-2) lets a model forget on a schedule but cannot make a precise targeted edit. The delta rule makes precise edits but cannot decide to forget. Each alone was insufficient.
mechanism: Combine them: a data-dependent decay gate for coarse forgetting, plus the delta rule for precise per-key overwriting, in one update. Fast erasure when the topic changes, surgical correction when a specific fact changes.
math:
S_t = S_{t−1}( α_t ( I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ ) ) + β_t v_t k_tᵀ
o_t = S_t q_t
math_note: Verbatim from the paper. α_t is the decay gate (coarse forgetting, from Mamba2's S_t = α_t S_{t−1} + v_t k_tᵀ) and β_t is the write strength of the delta rule. Both appear in one update, which is the whole contribution.
buys: Beats Mamba-2 and DeltaNet individually on language modelling, in-context retrieval and long-context tasks
The two mechanisms are genuinely complementary rather than redundant
Efficient chunkwise-parallel training algorithm
The practical winner of the linear-attention line — adopted in shipped hybrid models
costs: Still fixed-state, so full attention still wins on hard exact retrieval — this is the ceiling the entire family shares
Not used pure: the models that ship it interleave it with full-attention layers, which is a tacit admission that it is not sufficient alone
More complex than either component, with more to tune
Needs specialised kernels for its advertised speed
pick_when: As the cheap layer type in a hybrid stack — the standard is roughly three of these per full-attention layer. That ratio is the actual state of the art for long-context efficiency, and its existence is the honest verdict on pure linear attention.

name: Titans (test-time memory)
title_check: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
plain: Give the model a memory it keeps updating while it reads, writing down whatever surprised it. It adapts to the specific document, but updating weights while serving users is expensive and awkward.
problem: Attention is precise but bounded by its window; recurrent state is unbounded in reach but lossy. Could a model learn, at inference time, what is worth memorising?
mechanism: Add a neural long-term memory module updated by gradient descent *during inference*, using a surprise signal — how badly the memory predicted the current input — to decide what to write, with a forgetting gate to bound capacity.
buys: Memory that adapts to the specific sequence being processed, rather than being fixed at training time
Scales to very long contexts while outperforming baselines on needle-in-a-haystack tasks
Surprise-based writing is a principled criterion for what deserves storage
costs: Gradient updates at inference time are a substantial serving complexity and cost — a real barrier to deployment
State becomes request-dependent, which complicates batching and caching
Limited independent reproduction so far
The forgetting mechanism still means bounded capacity
pick_when: Not production-ready, but included because it is the clearest current attempt at the question the whole timeline is circling: not how to compress memory, but how to *decide* what is worth remembering.
confused_with: Dated 2025 in most write-ups because of its arXiv number (2501.*). The v1 submission is 31 December 2024.

name: Tensor Product Attention (TPA)
title_check: Tensor Product Attention Is All You Need
plain: Store the queries, keys and values in a factorised form rather than in full, so the cache shrinks a lot. Unlike the compression trick DeepSeek uses, this one fits together with rotary positions cleanly instead of needing an awkward extra dimension.
problem: Long context means a large KV cache, and the fixes so far either cost quality by making heads share (MQA, GQA) or, in MLA's case, collide awkwardly with RoPE and require a decoupled extra dimension to work around it.
mechanism: Use tensor decompositions to represent queries, keys and values as contextual low-rank components, so only the compact factors are cached and the full tensors are reconstructed when needed. The factorisation is designed to integrate with Rotary Position Embedding directly.
buys: Substantially smaller KV cache at inference, addressing the same bottleneck as MLA
Reported to match or beat MHA, MQA, GQA and MLA on perplexity and a range of benchmarks - a rare claim of better quality alongside less memory
Composes with RoPE without a decoupled dimension, which is the ugliest part of MLA's design
The memory saving translates into genuinely longer sequences under a fixed budget
costs: A pretraining-time architecture. Like MLA and unlike GQA, you cannot convert an existing checkpoint into it cheaply
The decomposition rank is a new hyperparameter, and it trades cache size against fidelity in a way that has to be tuned
More conceptually involved than head-sharing, which raises the bar for anyone implementing or debugging it
Adoption is far behind MLA, which has multiple frontier deployments. Reported benchmark wins and production evidence are not the same thing
pick_when: Worth serious consideration if you are designing a new model, want MLA-class cache savings, and would rather not inherit MLA's RoPE workaround. Stay with GQA if you need to adapt an existing checkpoint, and with MLA if you want the option with the most deployment evidence behind it.

name: Lightning Attention at scale (MiniMax-01)
title_check: MiniMax-01: Scaling Foundation Models with Lightning Attention
plain: The first convincing demonstration that fixed-memory attention holds up inside a very large production model. Tellingly, they still kept one full-attention layer for every seven cheap ones.
problem: Linear attention worked at research scale. Nobody had shown it holding up in a frontier-scale production model.
mechanism: An IO-aware linear attention implementation, deployed in a 456B-parameter MoE model in a hybrid schedule: seven lightning-attention layers for every one softmax layer, supporting up to 4M tokens.
buys: First convincing demonstration of linear attention at frontier scale
Context lengths far beyond what pure softmax models offered at the time
Establishes the hybrid ratio as the practical design pattern
costs: Even at 7:1 they kept softmax layers — pure linear was not viable, which is the finding, not a footnote
Enormous engineering investment that few organisations can replicate
Benchmarks at extreme context are hard to interpret and easy to overclaim
pick_when: As evidence for the hybrid pattern rather than as a component. The 7:1 ratio is a useful anchor next to Kimi Linear's 3:1.

name: Native Sparse Attention (NSA)
title_check: Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention
plain: Three views at once: a coarse summary of everything, a close look at the blocks that matter, and the nearby words, with the model trained from the start to work this way. Real measured speedups, but you cannot bolt it onto a model that is already finished.
problem: Sparse attention had always been bolted on at inference, creating a train/test mismatch, and its theoretical savings rarely survived contact with real GPU kernels.
mechanism: Three branches per query, combined by a learned gate: compressed coarse-grained blocks summarising the whole sequence; selected fine-grained blocks chosen by importance scores; and a sliding window for local context.
