Crucially it is trained this way from the start, and the kernels are designed around GPU memory access patterns.
buys: Trainable end to end, so the model learns to work with sparsity instead of having it imposed afterwards
Real measured speedups — up to 11.6× on 64K sequences — not just theoretical FLOP reductions
Matches or beats full attention on general benchmarks despite being sparse
The three branches cover distinct needs: global summary, precise retrieval, local detail
costs: Must be adopted at pretraining time; you cannot convert an existing dense model
Substantially more complex than any single-pattern scheme — three branches, a gate, and bespoke kernels
Block granularity means selection is coarse: you retrieve a block, not a token
Benefits appear mainly at long context; at short context the overhead is not worth it
pick_when: New long-context models where you control pretraining and need genuine sparsity that survives contact with hardware. This is the current state of the art for trainable sparsity, and 'hardware-aligned' is what distinguishes it from the 2019–2020 attempts.
confused_with: Probably what 'MSA' referred to in the spoken assignment brief, though MLA is a possible alternative reading. Both are covered here.

name: MoBA (Mixture of Block Attention)
title_check: MoBA: Mixture of Block Attention for Long-Context LLMs
plain: Split the past into blocks and let a learned router choose which blocks each question reads, the same way some models choose between experts. It can be switched back to full attention, so unlike NSA it can be added to an existing model.
problem: Sparse patterns are chosen by humans. Mixture-of-Experts had already shown that routing decisions can be learned — why not apply the same idea to which parts of the context to read?
mechanism: Partition the context into blocks and use an MoE-style top-k router so each query attends only to the blocks it selects. Because it can switch between sparse and full attention, it can be applied to existing models.
buys: Learned, content-dependent block selection rather than a fixed pattern
Can be switched between sparse and full modes, so it retrofits to existing models — a real advantage over NSA
Deployed in production, with large speedups at long context
costs: Block granularity is coarse, like NSA's
Routing can be unstable and may need load-balancing care, inheriting known MoE failure modes
The router is extra computation on every query
Sparse and full modes can behave differently, which is a subtle source of train/serve mismatch
pick_when: When you want learned sparsity but need to retrofit an existing model rather than pretrain. NSA is the stronger choice if you control pretraining.

name: Forgetting Transformer (FoX)
title_check: Forgetting Transformer: Softmax Attention with a Forget Gate
plain: Recurrent models have a forget gate and Transformers never did. This puts one inside ordinary softmax attention by quietly damping scores the model wants to ignore. It improves quality and needs no position encoding at all - but it does nothing about the cost.
problem: The forget gate is essential to every modern recurrent model, and a Transformer has no recurrent form to put one in. So the one mechanism that most clearly helped the linear-attention family had no equivalent in full attention.
mechanism: Down-weight the unnormalized attention scores in a data-dependent way before the softmax. That single change acts as a forget gate inside ordinary attention - the paper calls it Forgetting Attention - and because it modifies scores rather than the algorithm's structure, it remains compatible with FlashAttention.
buys: Beats the standard Transformer on long-context language modelling, length extrapolation and short-context downstream tasks, and matches it on long-context downstream tasks
Needs no positional embeddings at all - the gate supplies the recency structure that RoPE and ALiBi are usually there to provide
Compatible with FlashAttention, so it keeps the exact-attention speed that most attention modifications sacrifice
Retains full attention's advantage over Mamba-2, HGRN2 and DeltaNet on needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, which the fixed-state models lose
costs: Still quadratic. This improves quality, not cost - none of the bill that drives this timeline gets paid down

The paper's 'Pro' block, which contributes much of the reported gain, also improves the plain Transformer. Part of the headline improvement is therefore not attributable to the forget gate itself, and the paper is upfront about that
Adds a per-head data-dependent gate to train and tune
Recent, with limited independent replication at scale
pick_when: When long-context quality is the binding constraint and you can afford exact attention. It is the interesting counter-current on this timeline: almost everything after 2019 makes attention cheaper, and this takes an idea from the cheap models and spends it on making the expensive one better.
confused_with: Not a linear-attention method despite the forget gate. The gate lives inside softmax attention, and the cost stays quadratic - it borrows the idea from the recurrent family without joining it.

name: Multi-Token Attention (MTA)
title_check: Multi-Token Attention
plain: Normally one word's attention to another is decided by comparing exactly two vectors, which is a surprisingly thin channel. This lets neighbouring words influence each other's scores, so the model can use more evidence to decide what is relevant - at the cost of extra compute in every layer.
problem: An attention weight is determined by the similarity of a single query vector and a single key vector. That single-token bottleneck caps how much information is available for telling a relevant passage apart from a similar-looking irrelevant one.
mechanism: Apply convolution operations over queries, keys and heads, so nearby queries and keys influence one another's attention weights. A weight is then conditioned on several query and key vectors at once rather than on one pair.
buys: Attention decisions draw on richer evidence than a single vector pair can carry
Notably better on tasks that require finding information inside long contexts, which is exactly where single-token matching is weakest
Outperforms Transformer baselines on standard language modelling too, so the gain is not confined to retrieval
Slots into an existing Transformer without changing the surrounding architecture
costs: Convolutions over queries, keys and heads add parameters and compute to every attention layer
Still quadratic - like FoX, this buys quality rather than paying down the bill
The convolution window is a fixed design choice, which quietly reintroduces the hand-set locality prior that content-based attention existed to get rid of
Evaluated at modest scale relative to frontier models, so how it behaves at scale is untested
pick_when: When retrieval inside long context is the failure mode you are actually fighting and you have compute to spare. Not a fit if inference cost is your constraint, since it makes attention more expensive rather than less.

name: Log-Linear Attention
title_check: Log-Linear Attention
plain: Linear attention keeps one fixed-size memory and forgets detail; full attention keeps everything and costs the square of the length. This keeps a memory that grows slowly - logarithmically - landing in between. It is a genuinely new third option rather than a tweak to either end.
problem: Linear attention and state-space models give linear time and constant memory, but at their core they are still RNNs, and a fixed-size hidden state is a fundamental limit on what context can be represented. Softmax attention has no such limit and costs quadratic compute. Nothing occupied the middle.
mechanism: Replace the fixed-size hidden state with a logarithmically growing set of hidden states. With a particular growth function this still admits a matmul-rich parallel form, so compute is log-linear in sequence length rather than linear or quadratic. It is a framework rather than one model: it can be layered on top of existing linear-attention variants.
buys: A genuine third point on the map - O(n log n) compute and logarithmic memory, between linear attention's O(n) and softmax's O(n²)
Lifts the fixed-state ceiling that limits every model in the linear family, without paying full quadratic cost
Keeps the matmul-rich parallel form that makes linear attention trainable on modern hardware
A general framework: instantiated on both Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet, and reported to perform well against their linear-time versions
costs: Memory grows. The entire selling point of linear attention was a state that does not, and logarithmic growth is still growth - at extreme context this loses to a genuinely fixed state
The hierarchical state is materially more complex to implement than either endpoint it sits between
Demonstrated as case studies on two existing architectures rather than at frontier scale, so the practical envelope is not yet mapped
Adds a growth function to choose, which is a new design decision with no established default
pick_when: When a fixed-size state demonstrably loses too much on your task and quadratic attention costs too much to run - the honest middle that until 2025 did not exist. Its wider significance is that it reframes the choice: efficient attention had been treated as a binary between O(n) and O(n²), and this shows the space in between is real and reachable.

name: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA)
date_evidence: Released with DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp and announced in the DeepSeek API docs on 2025-09-29 (news250929); day-0 vLLM support the same day. The formal write-up appears later in the DeepSeek-V3.2 report, arXiv 2512.02556 (v1 2025-12-02). The mechanism's date is a product release, not a preprint.
plain: A small, cheap scorer skims the entire history and passes only the best couple of thousand words through to the real attention. Fine-grained, and it stacks with compressed storage; the risk is that the scorer itself ranks something wrongly and quietly drops it.
problem: NSA still selects at block granularity and carries three branches. Could selection be finer-grained and cheaper, and compose with MLA's compressed cache?
mechanism: A 'lightning indexer' — a small, low-precision scoring module keeping a tiny key cache per token (128 vs MLA's 512) — scores every previous token and passes only the top-k (around 2048) into sparse MLA. Selection is per token rather than per block, and the indexer is cheap enough to run over the full history.
buys: Fine-grained per-token selection rather than block granularity
Composes with MLA, so cache compression and sparsity stack
Large inference cost reduction at long context, which DeepSeek passed through as API price cuts — an unusually concrete efficiency claim
Indexer runs in FP8, so scoring the full history stays cheap
costs: Still O(n) indexer work per query — cheaper than O(n²) attention, but not free, and it grows with context
A separate indexer is another trained component that can misrank and silently drop needed context
Shipped as an experimental model, so long-term quality effects were not fully characterised at release
Deeply entangled with MLA, so it is not a portable drop-in
pick_when: The current frontier design for long-context serving if you are pretraining a model with MLA. Its top-k-with-a-cheap-indexer shape is the direct descendant of 2021's top-k attention, made affordable.
confused_with: DSA (DeepSeek Sparse Attention) is not NSA (Native Sparse Attention). Same lab, different mechanisms, seven months apart: NSA selects blocks with three branches, DSA selects tokens with an indexer feeding sparse MLA.

name: Kimi Linear / Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)
title_check: Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture
plain: Refines the forget dial so each channel of memory can fade at its own rate, used three cheap layers to every one full layer. Beats full attention on their tests while storing far less, and still cannot stand on its own.
problem: Gated DeltaNet's forget gate is coarse — one scalar decay for the whole state. Different channels should be able to forget at different rates.
mechanism: Kimi Delta Attention refines Gated DeltaNet with fine-grained channel-wise gating, deployed in a hybrid stack of three KDA layers to one full-attention MLA layer.
buys: Beats full attention on the reported benchmarks while using far less KV cache
Channel-wise gating is meaningfully more expressive than a single scalar decay
Validates the 3:1 hybrid ratio at scale
costs: Still keeps full-attention layers — the linear layers cannot stand alone, again
Finer gating means more parameters and more tuning surface
Needs specialised kernels
Recent enough that independent long-horizon evaluation is limited
pick_when: As the current best-documented instance of the hybrid pattern. Compare its 3:1 ratio against MiniMax-01's 7:1 — that ratio is the real design question now, not which single attention to use.

name: DroPE (dropping positional embeddings)
title_check: Extending the Context of Pretrained LLMs by Dropping Their Positional Embeddings
plain: Train the model with position information, then take it away and let it settle for a short while. It has already learned where words sit, so it now works far past its training length with no long-context training at all, provided you still have the original training data.
problem: RoPE helps a model learn position during pretraining, but at inference beyond the trained length its rotations drift out of distribution and warp long-range attention. Every rescaling method so far (PI, NTK-aware, YaRN) tries to repair RoPE. What if you removed it instead?
mechanism: Treat positional encoding as a transient training aid. Pretrain normally with RoPE, then drop it entirely and run a short recalibration on the original pretraining data *at the original context length*. The model has already learned positional structure in its Q and K projections and the causal mask supplies the rest, so it keeps working — and now generalises past its training length because there is no position-dependent rotation left to drift.
buys: Zero-shot context extension with no long-context finetuning at all — the expensive part of every other method is skipped
Reported to substantially outperform RoPE rescaling methods and purpose-built architectures on length extension
Recalibration happens at the original context length, so it is cheap
Removes the failure mode at its source instead of patching it: no rotations means no rotation drift
costs: Requires access to the pretraining data and a recalibration run — unavailable if you only have the weights
Dropping the encoding causes a sharp loss spike that must be annealed back down; get the schedule wrong and it does not recover
Timing is load-bearing: dropping late in pretraining works, dropping earlier steadily degrades results, so this is not a free post-hoc switch
Relies on the causal mask for implicit position, so it does not apply to encoder-style bidirectional models
Recent, with limited independent replication so far
pick_when: When you control pretraining and want long context without paying for long-context training — train short, drop, extend. If you only have downloaded weights and no data, YaRN remains the practical choice.
confused_with: CRITICAL: not the same as DRoPE, 'Directional Rotary Position Embedding for Efficient Agent Interaction Modeling' (arXiv 2503.15029, March 2025), which is an autonomous-driving trajectory-modelling paper with no connection to LLM context extension. The names differ only in capitalisation and the papers are nine months and one field apart.

name: HySparse (oracle token selection + KV sharing)
title_check: HySparse: A Hybrid Sparse Attention Architecture with Oracle Token Selection and KV Cache Sharing
plain: Let the cheap layers copy both their choices and their stored memory from the full-attention layer above, rather than each one guessing for itself. That cuts computation and memory together, which earlier sparse methods mostly failed to do.
problem: Two flaws had survived the whole sparse-attention line. Selecting which tokens matter needed a separate proxy module (NSA's branches, DSA's indexer, MoBA's router), which is extra complexity that can misrank. And sparse layers usually cut computation without cutting the KV cache at all — you still stored everything.
mechanism: Interleave each full-attention layer with several sparse layers, and have those sparse layers take both their token selection *and* their KV cache directly from the full-attention layer above them. The full layer acts as an exact oracle for what matters, so no separate scoring module is needed, and the sparse layers store nothing of their own.
buys: No separate importance proxy — the full attention layer already computed the answer, so selection is exact rather than predicted
Cuts computation and memory together, which prior sparse designs mostly failed to do
Reported ~10× KV cache reduction on an 80B MoE with only 5 of 49 layers using full attention
Reported to beat both full attention and sliding-window hybrid baselines
costs: Sparse layers are now structurally coupled to the full layer above them, so the layer schedule is a hard architectural constraint rather than a free choice
Reusing an upper layer's selection assumes different layers want the same tokens, which is an approximation and will not always hold
A pretraining-time architecture, not a retrofit
Very recent, so independent replication is limited
pick_when: New long-context models where KV memory is the binding constraint. Its idea — stop paying for a separate indexer, reuse what full attention already told you — is the cleanest answer yet to a cost every sparse method before it paid.

name: Kwai Summary Attention (KSA)
title_check: Kwai Summary Attention Technical Report
plain: Rather than chasing the smallest possible memory, compress the history by a fixed factor into summary words. Deliberately not the cheapest option: it spends some memory to keep the distant past legible and inspectable.
problem: The field had split into two camps, and both have a ceiling. Shrinking the per-layer cache (GQA, MLA) still leaves the cache growing 1:1 with sequence length. Interleaving cache-friendly layers (sliding window, Gated DeltaNet) trades away long-context fidelity. Neither camp questioned whether 'as small as possible' was the right target.
mechanism: Take the middle path nobody had explored: keep the cache linear in sequence length, but divide it by a compression ratio k by folding history into learnable summary tokens. Cost becomes O(n/k) rather than O(n) or O(1).
buys: Deliberately does not chase a minimum cache, and buys back complete and referential retention of distant dependencies for a bounded memory cost
Summary tokens are interpretable — you can inspect what was retained, unlike a linear model's opaque state vector
k is a single dial trading memory against fidelity, rather than an architectural commitment
Avoids the recall cliff that fixed-state methods hit
costs: Still linear in sequence length, so it does not reach the flat memory profile of linear attention — at extreme context it loses to a fixed state
Summary compression is lossy by construction; detail inside a summarised span is gone
Adds learnable summary tokens that must be trained, so it is not a drop-in
A single technical report, and not yet independently replicated
pick_when: When O(1) state loses too much and O(n) costs too much — the honest middle. Notable mainly for rejecting the framing that everyone else accepted, which is usually where the next idea comes from.

name: BFLA (block-filtered long-context attention)
title_check: BFLA: Block-Filtered Long-Context Attention Mechanism
plain: Cheaply estimate which blocks of a long prompt matter, then skip the rest while reading it. It needs no retraining whatsoever so anyone can use it, but it only speeds up reading the prompt, not writing the answer.
problem: Every trainable sparse method (NSA, DSA, HySparse) demands that you control pretraining. Anyone holding downloaded weights was locked out of sparsity entirely, and long prompts stayed expensive to prefill.
mechanism: Two training-free stages. First, compress queries and keys into coarse blocks and cheaply estimate each block's share of the softmax mass, giving an input-dependent importance mask. Second, expand that mask onto the Triton attention-tile grid, with tile-level rescue strategies to limit information loss, and skip unimportant KV tiles in a fused kernel while keeping attention exact inside every tile retained.
buys: Completely training-free: no retraining, calibration, preprocessing or model modification
Drops into existing vLLM-style paged-attention serving stacks
Attention stays exact within every retained tile, so the loss is only from what was skipped
Demonstrated across several current open-weight model families
costs: Prefill only — it accelerates processing a long prompt, not the decoding that follows
Skipped tiles are a genuine approximation; accuracy degrades, and the paper claims 'minimal', not 'none'
Block-mass estimation is a heuristic that can misjudge which blocks matter
Tied to Triton kernels and tile geometry, so portability is limited
pick_when: You have weights you cannot retrain, long prompts, and prefill latency is hurting. This is the accessible counterpart to NSA/DSA — worse in principle, but usable by everyone rather than only by labs that pretrain.

name: FlashMorph (learned hybrid layer selection)
title_check: Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models
plain: Everyone agrees the answer is a mixture of cheap and expensive layers, but nobody knew which layers should be which. This searches for the combination rather than guessing, treating it as one joint decision instead of judging each layer alone.
problem: By 2026 everyone agrees the answer is a hybrid — some full-attention layers, the rest linear. But which layers stay full? MiniMax-01 chose 7:1, Kimi Linear chose 3:1, and both picked placement by heuristic. Existing methods score layers in isolation, ignoring that the right choice for one layer depends on every other choice.
mechanism: Treat layer selection as a budget-constrained subset optimisation. Build a 'morphable' model where every full-attention layer also carries a converted linear branch, freeze all weights, and jointly train per-layer gates on synthetic long-context retrieval data with a regulariser pushing towards linear. Discretise the learned gates under a full-attention budget, then distil and finetune.
buys: Optimises the layer schedule jointly, capturing interdependence that per-layer scoring misses
Finds better hybrid configurations than heuristic placement while costing far less to search
Preserves long-context recall and general benchmark performance
Turns 'how many full layers, and where' from folklore into something measured
costs: A conversion method, so it inherits whatever the base Transformer's ceiling is
Gates are trained on synthetic retrieval data, and that proxy may not match the real workload
Multi-stage — morph, gate-train, discretise, distil, finetune — so it is a pipeline, not a switch
Still needs a full-attention budget chosen by a human up front
pick_when: Converting an existing Transformer into a hybrid, rather than pretraining one. It is the clearest sign of where the field now is: the open question is no longer which attention mechanism to use, but how to schedule several of them across depth.
